claim: The cerebellum is a well-conserved structure across species and particularly across mammals.
source: The cerebellum is a well-conserved structure across species and particularly across mammals.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about cerebellar anatomy.

claim: The cerebellar cortex is organized in three layers: the molecular layer, the Purkinje layer, and the granular layer.
source: The cerebellar cortex is a highly folded structure organised in three layers: the molecular layer (containing the notable Purkinje cell dendritic trees), the Purkinje layer (containing the somas of Purkinje cells), and the granular layer (containing the granule cells).
evidence: This is stated as established anatomical knowledge about cerebellar structure.

claim: The cerebellum contains more than half of the total brain neurons.
source: Despite its small size (compared to the cerebrum), it contains more than half of the total brain neurons: this is mainly due to the granule cells, very small and densely packed cells, some of the smallest of the brain, presenting a very simple morphology (Haines and Dietrichs, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Haines and Dietrichs, 2012.

claim: Granule cells are some of the smallest cells in the brain.
source: Despite its small size (compared to the cerebrum), it contains more than half of the total brain neurons: this is mainly due to the granule cells, very small and densely packed cells, some of the smallest of the brain, presenting a very simple morphology (Haines and Dietrichs, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Haines and Dietrichs, 2012.

claim: Purkinje cells are one of the largest types of neurons and most complex cells in the brain.
source: On the other hand, the Purkinje cells are one of the largest types of neurons and most complex cells in the brain.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Purkinje cell characteristics.

claim: Cerebellar development is protracted, starting from birth to a few weeks old in rodents.
source: Cerebellar development is protracted (Szulc et al., 2015), starting from birth (or the last trimester of pregnancy) to a few weeks old in rodents (or 2 y.o. in humans) (Sathyanesan et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Szulc et al., 2015 and Sathyanesan et al., 2019.

claim: The cerebellum is involved in many basic and high-level functions, from motor control to social skills.
source: The cerebellum is involved in many basic and high-level functions, from motor control to social skills, and it is known to be affected in a number of neurodevelopmental disorders (Stoodley, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stoodley, 2016.

claim: The cerebellum is affected in a number of neurodevelopmental disorders.
source: The cerebellum is involved in many basic and high-level functions, from motor control to social skills, and it is known to be affected in a number of neurodevelopmental disorders (Stoodley, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Stoodley, 2016.

claim: In rodents, Purkinje cells' dendritic trees start growing at birth.
source: In rodents, Purkinje cells' dendritic trees start growing at birth.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Purkinje cell development in rodents.

claim: In 30 days, Purkinje cells evolve from a simple soma (~10 µm diameter) to a large cell with a highly branched and planar dendritic tree (soma diameter ~20 µm, area ~10,000 µm2 in the mouse).
source: In 30 days, they evolve from a simple soma (~10 µm diameter) to a large cell with a highly branched and planar dendritic tree (soma diameter ~20 µm, area ~10,000 µm2 in the mouse; Beekhof et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Beekhof et al., 2021.

claim: Purkinje cell morphology can be altered in autism spectrum disorders (ASD), as shown post-mortem in humans.
source: Purkinje cell morphology can be altered in autism spectrum disorders (ASD), as shown post-mortem, in humans (Fatemi et al., 2002) and multiple mouse models of ASD.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fatemi et al., 2002.

claim: Tsc1 mutant mice show increased spine density in Purkinje cells.
source: Specifically, they show an increased spine density in Tsc1 mutant mice (Tsai et al., 2012), an overgrowth of the dendritic tree and abnormal branching in PTEN KO mice (Cupolillo et al., 2016), a reduction of the dendritic tree in AUTS2 mice (Yamashiro et al., 2020), and general alterations in developmental disorders (Kim et al., 2011; Robinson et al., 2012; Usui et al., 2017; Sundberg et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tsai et al., 2012.

claim: PTEN KO mice show overgrowth of the dendritic tree and abnormal branching in Purkinje cells.
source: Specifically, they show an increased spine density in Tsc1 mutant mice (Tsai et al., 2012), an overgrowth of the dendritic tree and abnormal branching in PTEN KO mice (Cupolillo et al., 2016), a reduction of the dendritic tree in AUTS2 mice (Yamashiro et al., 2020), and general alterations in developmental disorders (Kim et al., 2011; Robinson et al., 2012; Usui et al., 2017; Sundberg et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cupolillo et al., 2016.

claim: AUTS2 mice show a reduction of the dendritic tree in Purkinje cells.
source: Specifically, they show an increased spine density in Tsc1 mutant mice (Tsai et al., 2012), an overgrowth of the dendritic tree and abnormal branching in PTEN KO mice (Cupolillo et al., 2016), a reduction of the dendritic tree in AUTS2 mice (Yamashiro et al., 2020), and general alterations in developmental disorders (Kim et al., 2011; Robinson et al., 2012; Usui et al., 2017; Sundberg et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yamashiro et al., 2020.

claim: All cerebellar outputs transit via the deep cerebellar nuclei.
source: All cerebellar outputs transit via the deep cerebellar nuclei, and a couple of them project to the thalamus before spreading to the cortex.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about cerebellar connectivity.

claim: The thalamus is considered a relay station in the brain and contains about 60 nuclei on unique pathways.
source: The thalamus is considered a relay station in the brain and contains about 60 nuclei on unique pathways.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about thalamic anatomy.

claim: The microstructure of the mediodorsal nucleus and the pulvinar nucleus is altered in schizophrenia and psychosis.
source: Some thalamic nuclei are involved in psychiatric disorders, and more specifically, the microstructure of the mediodorsal nucleus and the pulvinar nucleus is altered in schizophrenia and psychosis (Hwang et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hwang et al., 2022.

claim: The lateral reticular nuclei are involved in ASD.
source: Some other nuclei are involved in neurodevelopmental disorders (e.g. the lateral reticular nuclei in ASD; Krol et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Krol et al., 2018.

claim: Thalamocortical projections are crucial for the cytoarchitectural development of the cortex.
source: Thalamocortical projections are crucial for the cytoarchitectural development of the cortex (Antón-Bolaños et al., 2018; Sato et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Antón-Bolaños et al., 2018 and Sato et al., 2022.

claim: Schizophrenia has a neurodevelopmental origin.
source: Neurodevelopmental disorders, or even psychiatric disorders with a neurodevelopmental origin, such as schizophrenia (Fatemi and Folsom, 2009), generally need better neurobiological characterisation during development (Ismail and Shapiro, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fatemi and Folsom, 2009.

claim: Manganese-enhanced MRI (MEMRI) is particularly suited to studying whole-brain early development in rodents.
source: Manganese-enhanced MRI (MEMRI) is particularly suited to studying whole-brain early development in rodents.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about MEMRI applications.

claim: MEMRI provides high structural contrast and a fast acquisition time in neonates.
source: It provides high structural contrast and a fast acquisition time in neonates (Szulc et al., 2015; Qiu et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Szulc et al., 2015 and Qiu et al., 2018.

claim: MEMRI is blind to the microstructural changes that lead to volumetric changes.
source: Still, the method is blind to the microstructural changes that lead to the volumetric changes reported.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of MEMRI based on the nature of the technique.

claim: Diffusion-weighted MRI (dMRI) measures the diffusion properties of water in the brain.
source: Diffusion-weighted MRI (dMRI) measures the diffusion properties of water in the brain: restricted and hindered by cell membranes, water diffusion provides an indirect measure of the tissue microstructure (Alexander et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Alexander et al., 2019.

claim: Water diffusion provides an indirect measure of tissue microstructure.
source: Diffusion-weighted MRI (dMRI) measures the diffusion properties of water in the brain: restricted and hindered by cell membranes, water diffusion provides an indirect measure of the tissue microstructure (Alexander et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Alexander et al., 2019.

claim: High cortical fractional anisotropy (FA) at birth correlates with the presence of radial glia.
source: Comparison with post-mortem microscopy shows a correlation between a high cortical fractional anisotropy (FA) at birth and the presence of radial glia.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from comparison with post-mortem microscopy.

claim: Radial glia progressively disappears in the first week along with an FA decrease.
source: The latter progressively disappears in the first week along with an FA decrease, illustrating the potential of dMRI to characterise neurodevelopment (Hüppi, 2010; Chokshi et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hüppi, 2010 and Chokshi et al., 2011.

claim: Brain metabolites are mostly intracellular.
source: Brain metabolites are mostly intracellular, with some more specific to neurons (e.g. N-acetyl-aspartate [NAA] and glutamate [Glu]) and others more specific to glial cells (e.g. choline compounds, tCho, and myo-inositol, Ins); therefore, different cellular compartments can be resolved (Ronen and Valette, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ronen and Valette, 2015.

claim: N-acetyl-aspartate (NAA) and glutamate (Glu) are more specific to neurons.
source: Brain metabolites are mostly intracellular, with some more specific to neurons (e.g. N-acetyl-aspartate [NAA] and glutamate [Glu]) and others more specific to glial cells (e.g. choline compounds, tCho, and myo-inositol, Ins); therefore, different cellular compartments can be resolved (Ronen and Valette, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ronen and Valette, 2015.

claim: Choline compounds (tCho) and myo-inositol (Ins) are more specific to glial cells.
source: Brain metabolites are mostly intracellular, with some more specific to neurons (e.g. N-acetyl-aspartate [NAA] and glutamate [Glu]) and others more specific to glial cells (e.g. choline compounds, tCho, and myo-inositol, Ins); therefore, different cellular compartments can be resolved (Ronen and Valette, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ronen and Valette, 2015.

claim: Metabolites are 10^4-fold less concentrated than water.
source: However, metabolites are 104-fold less concentrated than water, requiring large measurement volumes for dMRS (typically ~50–100 mm3 in rodents), and long acquisition times.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about metabolite concentrations.

claim: Cellular morphological parameters estimated from dMRS correlate with neuronal and glial morphologies extracted from histological measures in the healthy, adult mouse.
source: Using multiple diffusion times and a post hoc model, cellular morphological parameters can be estimated from dMRS (Ligneul et al., 2024). They correlate with neuronal and glial morphologies extracted from histological measures in the healthy, adult mouse (Palombo et al., 2016; Palombo et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Palombo et al., 2016 and Palombo et al., 2017.

claim: Myo-inositol diffusion properties reflect astrocytic morphology in an induced model of astrocytic hypertrophy.
source: More specifically, it has been shown that myo-inositol diffusion properties reflect astrocytic morphology in an induced model of astrocytic hypertrophy (Ligneul et al., 2019) and in a mouse model of demyelination where astrocytic activation was expected (Genovese et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ligneul et al., 2019.

claim: Choline compound diffusion properties were associated with microglial activation in human disease.
source: Choline compound diffusion properties were associated with microglial activation in human disease (Ercan et al., 2016) or in an LPS-induced brain inflammation model (de Marco et al., 2022).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ercan et al., 2016.

claim: The cerebellum expands greatly after birth, when the Purkinje cells' dendritic trees start growing.
source: As described above, the cerebellum expands greatly after birth, when the Purkinje cells' dendritic trees start growing.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about cerebellar development.

claim: The slow maturation of the cerebellum exposes it longer to developmental insults.
source: This slow maturation exposes the cerebellum longer to developmental insults.
evidence: This is an inference based on the protracted development timeline.

claim: The thalamus develops relatively quickly compared to the cerebellum.
source: In contrast to the cerebellum, the thalamus develops relatively quickly, and its neurons expand and complexify more rapidly (Szulc et al., 2015; Takeuchi et al., 2014; Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Szulc et al., 2015 and Takeuchi et al., 2014, and referenced in Figure 1A.

claim: Both cerebellar and thalamic volumes are just below 50 µl at P5.
source: Both cerebellar and thalamic volumes are just below 50 µl at P5 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The cerebellum triples in volume between P5 and P30.
source: The cerebellum triples in volume, between P5 and P30, reaching 90% of its P30 volume at P20, while the thalamus reaches 90% of the P30 volume at P15.
evidence: This is based on volumetric measurements from MEMRI data.

claim: The cerebellum reaches 90% of its P30 volume at P20.
source: The cerebellum triples in volume, between P5 and P30, reaching 90% of its P30 volume at P20, while the thalamus reaches 90% of the P30 volume at P15.
evidence: This is based on volumetric measurements from MEMRI data.

claim: The thalamus reaches 90% of the P30 volume at P15.
source: The cerebellum triples in volume, between P5 and P30, reaching 90% of its P30 volume at P20, while the thalamus reaches 90% of the P30 volume at P15.
evidence: This is based on volumetric measurements from MEMRI data.

claim: The metabolic profile changes noticeably between P5 and P30.
source: The metabolic profile changes noticeably between P5 and P30 as shown in Figure 3A.
evidence: This claim is supported by spectroscopic data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Between P5 and P30, apparent metabolite concentrations increase for tNAA, Glu, Gln, and Ins.
source: Between P5 and P30, apparent metabolite concentrations increase for tNAA, Glu, Gln, and Ins, and decrease for PE and Tau (only in the thalamus).
evidence: This is based on metabolite quantification from spectroscopic data.

claim: Between P5 and P30, apparent metabolite concentrations decrease for PE and Tau (only in the thalamus).
source: Between P5 and P30, apparent metabolite concentrations increase for tNAA, Glu, Gln, and Ins, and decrease for PE and Tau (only in the thalamus).
evidence: This is based on metabolite quantification from spectroscopic data.

claim: The increase in tNAA concentration with age is protracted in the cerebellum compared to thalamus.
source: Note that the increase in tNAA concentration with age is protracted in the cerebellum compared to thalamus and has not reached a plateau at P30.
evidence: This is based on metabolite quantification from spectroscopic data.

claim: For most metabolites, the signal attenuation is stronger in the thalamus, suggesting less restricted diffusion compared to the cerebellum.
source: For most metabolites (except tCho), the signal attenuation is stronger in the thalamus, suggesting less restricted diffusion compared to the cerebellum.
evidence: This is based on diffusion-weighted MRS measurements and interpretation.

claim: There is a trend for lower signal attenuation and lower ADCs with increasing age, suggesting increasing restriction of metabolite diffusion.
source: There is also a trend for lower signal attenuation and lower ADCs with increasing age for some metabolites, suggesting increasing restriction of metabolite diffusion.
evidence: This is based on diffusion-weighted MRS measurements and interpretation.

claim: The trend for lower signal attenuation and lower ADCs with increasing age is particularly striking for Tau in the thalamus.
source: This is particularly striking for Tau in the thalamus.
evidence: This is based on diffusion-weighted MRS measurements.

claim: Sphere fraction differs significantly between regions for tNAA and Glu.
source: Between regions, sphere fraction differs significantly (Table 1).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of biophysical modeling results shown in Table 1.

claim: The general trend for Ins is a high sphere fraction (~0.7–0.9).
source: The general trend is a high sphere fraction (~0.7–0.9) for Ins and moderately high (~0.5–0.6) for tCho.
evidence: This is based on biophysical modeling results.

claim: The general trend for tCho is a moderately high sphere fraction (~0.5–0.6).
source: The general trend is a high sphere fraction (~0.7–0.9) for Ins and moderately high (~0.5–0.6) for tCho.
evidence: This is based on biophysical modeling results.

claim: The radius estimated from tCho differs significantly between regions.
source: The radius estimated from tCho differs significantly between regions.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of biophysical modeling results.

claim: There is a trend of decreasing sphere fraction in the cerebellum with age for glial markers.
source: Note the trend of decreasing sphere fraction in the cerebellum with age.
evidence: This is based on biophysical modeling results.

claim: The sphere fraction differs significantly between regions for both tCr and Tau.
source: Between regions, the sphere fraction differs significantly for both metabolites (Table 1), but only Tau exhibits a significant change with age, and this change is different between regions (significant interaction term).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of biophysical modeling results shown in Table 1.

claim: Only Tau exhibits a significant change in sphere fraction with age, and this change is different between regions.
source: Between regions, the sphere fraction differs significantly for both metabolites (Table 1), but only Tau exhibits a significant change with age, and this change is different between regions (significant interaction term).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of biophysical modeling results shown in Table 1.

claim: For Tau, the radius is significantly different between regions, changes significantly with age, and this change is different between regions.
source: For Tau, the radius is significantly different between regions, changes significantly with age, and this change is different between regions (significant interaction term).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of biophysical modeling results.

claim: A study of human WM using diffusion MRI reported an increase in FA and a decrease in MD with age in early life.
source: A study of human WM using diffusion MRI reported an increase in FA and a decrease in MD with age in early life (Hüppi, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hüppi, 2010.

claim: In mice, the same relationship (increase in FA and decrease in MD with age) was found in both WM and GM.
source: In mice, the same relationship was found in both WM and GM (Chahboune et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chahboune et al., 2009.

claim: fsphere(tCr, Tau) decreases with age in the cerebellum.
source: fsphere(tCr, Tau) decreases with age in the cerebellum, meaning that tCr and Tau are located in compartments where the relative contribution of sphere-like structures (e.g. cell-bodies) decreases.
evidence: This is based on biophysical modeling results.

claim: The decrease in fsphere(tCr, Tau) with age in the cerebellum reflects cerebellar cell growth and complexification.
source: In other words, it reflects cerebellar cell growth and complexification (Figure 4A, Figure 5A).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the biophysical modeling results shown in Figures 4A and 5A.

claim: In the cerebellum, soma morphological maturation mostly happens in the first week.
source: In the cerebellum, while soma morphological maturation mostly happens in the first week (McKay and Turner, 2005), Purkinje cell dendritic expansion is rapid before P15 but then continues to mature up to the end of the 4th week (McKay and Turner, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to McKay and Turner, 2005.

claim: Purkinje cell dendritic expansion is rapid before P15 but then continues to mature up to the end of the 4th week.
source: In the cerebellum, while soma morphological maturation mostly happens in the first week (McKay and Turner, 2005), Purkinje cell dendritic expansion is rapid before P15 but then continues to mature up to the end of the 4th week (McKay and Turner, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to McKay and Turner, 2005.

claim: In cats, Tau dietary deficiency delays cortical and cerebellar maturation.
source: Tau diffusion properties might reflect the development of Purkinje cells: (i) in cats, which cannot synthesise Tau and must source it from their diet, Tau dietary deficiency delays cortical and cerebellar maturation (Aerts and Van Assche, 2002), meaning that Tau is also crucial in early development, and (ii) in the cerebellum, immunohistochemistry studies locate Tau in adult Purkinje cells (Madsen et al., 1985; Magnusson et al., 1988; Hussy et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Aerts and Van Assche, 2002.

claim: Immunohistochemistry studies locate Tau in adult Purkinje cells in the cerebellum.
source: Tau diffusion properties might reflect the development of Purkinje cells: (i) in cats, which cannot synthesise Tau and must source it from their diet, Tau dietary deficiency delays cortical and cerebellar maturation (Aerts and Van Assche, 2002), meaning that Tau is also crucial in early development, and (ii) in the cerebellum, immunohistochemistry studies locate Tau in adult Purkinje cells (Madsen et al., 1985; Magnusson et al., 1988; Hussy et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Madsen et al., 1985, Magnusson et al., 1988, and Hussy et al., 2000.

claim: High Tau levels are still detected in the cerebellum at P30.
source: These observations align well too with the high Tau levels we still detect in the cerebellum at P30 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is based on metabolite quantification shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The diffusion properties of glial metabolites, fsphere(Ins) and fsphere(tCho), tend to decrease with age.
source: The diffusion properties of glial metabolites, fsphere(Ins) and fsphere(tCho), also tend to decrease with age.
evidence: This is based on biophysical modeling results.

claim: Bergmann glia develop long processes along Purkinje cells.
source: This could be explained by another cerebellar peculiarity: Bergmann glia develop long processes along Purkinje cells, and this specific growth could contribute to the fsphere(tCr,Tau) decrease.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about Bergmann glia development.

claim: The evolution of fsphere,LT trend with age is comparable to fsphere(tCr).
source: The evolution of fsphere,LT trend with age is comparable to fsphere(tCr).
evidence: This is based on comparison of biophysical modeling results with literature-derived estimates.

claim: fsphere(Tau) values are overall lower than fsphere(tCr) and below fsphere,LT values.
source: Although fsphere(tCr) and fsphere(Tau) have similar trends, fsphere(Tau) values are overall lower and below fsphere,LT values (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on comparison of biophysical modeling results shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Tau is preferentially located in cerebellar neurons during cerebellar development.
source: This lends weight to the idea that Tau is preferentially located in cerebellar neurons during cerebellar development (and potentially less so in granule cells).
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparison of fsphere values.

claim: Tau has a higher Dintra compared to the other metabolites.
source: Note that Tau has a higher Dintra (Ligneul and Valette, 2017) compared to the other metabolites, potentially affecting the parameter estimation given for Tau.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ligneul and Valette, 2017.

claim: The fit for Tau was substantially improved for Dintra >0.6 µm2/ms.
source: As described in Methods, the fit for Tau was substantially improved for Dintra >0.6 µm2/ms.
evidence: This is based on model fitting results described in the Methods section.

claim: The evolution with age of (R,fsphere) is very similar for tNAA and Tau when Dintra = 0.7 µm2/ms.
source: Additionally, the evolution with age of (R,fsphere) is then very similar for tNAA and Tau, reinforcing the idea that Tau is neuronal in the cerebellum.
evidence: This is based on biophysical modeling results with adjusted Dintra.

claim: The decrease in Tau content in the thalamus points towards a change of compartmentation with age.
source: In the thalamus, the decrease in Tau content (Figure 3B) and the change in Tau diffusion properties (Figure 4B) point towards a change of compartmentation with age.
evidence: This is based on metabolite quantification and diffusion measurements shown in Figures 3B and 4B.

claim: fsphere(Tau) consistently increases with age in the thalamus.
source: Contrary to the trend in the cerebellum, fsphere(Tau) consistently increases with age in the thalamus (Figure 4—figure supplement 8).
evidence: This is based on biophysical modeling results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 8.

claim: Neurons are already branched at P10 in the thalamus.
source: Neurons are already branched at P10 in the thalamus (Takeuchi et al., 2014) (shown by a low fsphere(tNAA, Glu) at P10).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Takeuchi et al., 2014 and by the study's own data.

claim: fsphere(Tau) at P10 nears fsphere(tNAA, Glu), indicating that Tau might be located in neuronal compartments in the neonatal thalamus.
source: fsphere(Tau) at P10 nears fsphere(tNAA, Glu), indicating that Tau might be located in neuronal compartments in the neonatal thalamus.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of fsphere values.

claim: Tau contributes to neuronal proliferation in vitro.
source: Although this hypothesis is not verifiable in existing literature, some in vitro studies show that Tau contributes to neuronal proliferation (Hernández-Benítez et al., 2010) and neuronal growth (Mersman et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hernández-Benítez et al., 2010.

claim: Tau contributes to neuronal growth in vitro.
source: Although this hypothesis is not verifiable in existing literature, some in vitro studies show that Tau contributes to neuronal proliferation (Hernández-Benítez et al., 2010) and neuronal growth (Mersman et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mersman et al., 2020.

claim: At P30, fsphere(Tau) is closer to fsphere(tCho, Ins), indicating that Tau might be located in glial compartments in adulthood.
source: At P30, fsphere(Tau) is closer to fsphere(tCho, Ins), indicating that Tau might be located in glial compartments in adulthood.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of fsphere values.

claim: Immunohistochemistry studies locate Tau in adult thalamic glia.
source: Indeed, immunohistochemistry studies locate Tau in adult thalamic glia (Hussy et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hussy et al., 2000.

claim: Both tCr and Tau have high spectroscopic signals in neonates.
source: We confirm in this study the observation from Tkác et al., 2003, that both tCr and Tau have high spectroscopic signals in neonates.
evidence: This is based on the study's spectroscopic data and confirms a previous observation from Tkác et al., 2003.

claim: tCr and Tau are the two metabolites most reliably quantified up to P15 in both regions.
source: They are the two metabolites most reliably quantified up to P15 in both regions (continuing for Tau in the cerebellum up to P30), and the estimates of their diffusion properties are the most confident, contrary to the usual neuronal markers, tNAA and Glu.
evidence: This is based on the study's spectroscopic data quality assessment.

claim: There is no indication of a preferential neuronal compartmentation for tCr during early development.
source: However, there is no indication of a preferential neuronal compartmentation for this metabolite during early development; hence, it is less specific to neurons and probably even less to Purkinje cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the study's diffusion measurements.

claim: Tau seems to switch compartments in the thalamus between birth and adulthood.
source: Because Tau seems to switch compartments in the thalamus between birth and adulthood, we do not think its diffusion properties reliably inform thalamic neuronal morphological development.
evidence: This is an inference based on the study's diffusion measurements.

claim: In human brain, Tau content increases at birth and then decreases with age.
source: In both human (Hüppi et al., 1991; Pouwels et al., 1999) and rhesus monkey (Sturman et al., 1980) brains, Tau content increases at birth and then decreases with age and is therefore a marker of the immature brain in both species.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hüppi et al., 1991 and Pouwels et al., 1999.

claim: In rhesus monkey brain, Tau content increases at birth and then decreases with age.
source: In both human (Hüppi et al., 1991; Pouwels et al., 1999) and rhesus monkey (Sturman et al., 1980) brains, Tau content increases at birth and then decreases with age and is therefore a marker of the immature brain in both species.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sturman et al., 1980.

claim: Tau is a marker of the immature brain in both human and rhesus monkey.
source: In both human (Hüppi et al., 1991; Pouwels et al., 1999) and rhesus monkey (Sturman et al., 1980) brains, Tau content increases at birth and then decreases with age and is therefore a marker of the immature brain in both species.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited studies showing Tau content changes with age.

claim: Tau concentration is low in the adult human brain.
source: Although Tau concentration is low in the adult human brain, it is more concentrated in the cerebellum in adulthood (Pouwels et al., 1999; Emir et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pouwels et al., 1999 and Emir et al., 2012.

claim: Tau is more concentrated in the cerebellum in adulthood in humans.
source: Although Tau concentration is low in the adult human brain, it is more concentrated in the cerebellum in adulthood (Pouwels et al., 1999; Emir et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pouwels et al., 1999 and Emir et al., 2012.

claim: A similar finding of higher Tau in cerebellum was made in the adult rhesus monkey brain.
source: A similar finding was made in the adult rhesus monkey brain (Sturman et al., 1980), indicating a conserved pattern across species of Tau properties in the cerebellum.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sturman et al., 1980.

claim: There is a protracted increase in tNAA signal in the cerebellum compared to the thalamus.
source: We also observed a protracted increase in tNAA signal in the cerebellum compared to the thalamus.
evidence: This is based on the study's metabolite quantification data.

claim: dMRS is a normalised measure and dMRS outcomes are not affected by the neuronal density.
source: In contrast, we want to reiterate that dMRS is a normalised measure and dMRS outcomes are not affected by the neuronal density: they represent the average morphological properties of the cell types the metabolite belongs to.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the dMRS method.

claim: The mixing time used for the acquisition of signal decay at high b-values (TM = 100 ms) is too long to enable sensitivity to fibre radius.
source: The mixing time used for the acquisition of signal decay at high b-values (TM = 100 ms) is too long to enable sensitivity to fibre radius (Ligneul et al., 2024), hence the choice of 'astrosticks' model.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ligneul et al., 2024.

claim: The RMSEs from the different models tested tend to be more similar at P30, suggesting that it is less important to add a sphere compartment for modelling metabolites diffusion in the adult brain.
